summary: Specifies mechanisms for backward compatibility between Ethernet VPN (EVPN) and PBB-EVPN and the older VPLS and PBB-VPLS solutions. It also describes how both technologies can coexist in the same MPLS/IP network, per VPN instance, so providers can introduce EVPN gradually. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A company adopting a new phone system can run it alongside the old one while employees move over gradually. This document explains how the old and new network services can work together.

questions: how to migrate from vpls to evpn
subtitle: How new EVPN routers can join an existing VPLS network without touching the old routers.

tldr.problem: Service providers running VPLS and PBB-VPLS networks want to adopt EVPN and PBB-EVPN without upgrading any of their existing equipment.
tldr.mechanism: All the logic lives on the new EVPN PEs. They advertise both VPLS and EVPN discovery routes, build pseudowires to VPLS-only peers, and use EVPN tunnels to other EVPN PEs, in single-active redundancy mode.
tldr.outcome: EVPN and VPLS can share one MPLS/IP network per VPN instance, so sites can be migrated one at a time. All-active redundancy across the two kinds of PE is out of scope.

today: RFC 8560 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this RFC.

sections.title: Why Mix EVPN and VPLS
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) and Provider Backbone Bridging VPLS (PBB-VPLS) are widely deployed Layer 2 VPN technologies. Providers who want EVPN and PBB-EVPN also want to keep their existing investment, so they need a way to add EVPN to a brownfield network without any software or hardware upgrade to it.

This RFC specifies the control-plane and forwarding behavior for three things: auto-discovery of a VPN instance, unicast and multicast operation, and MAC mobility. It uses the shorthand (PBB-)EVPN and (PBB-)VPLS to cover both flavors.

The RFC covers VPLS with EVPN (Section 3) and PBB-VPLS with PBB-EVPN (Section 4). It does not cover PBB-VPLS with EVPN or VPLS with PBB-EVPN, because providers have not asked for them. The expected evolution paths are PBB-VPLS to PBB-EVPN and VPLS to EVPN.
sections.eli5: Some companies have an old network and want a new one. They do not want to replace everything at once, so this document lets old and new work side by side.

sections.title: Requirements for Coexistence
sections.content:
The RFC sets out requirements for backward compatibility. The most important ones are:

  • Migration must be possible in stages, site by site, per VPN instance.
  • No change to existing VPLS or PBB-VPLS PEs is allowed, not even a software upgrade.
  • (PBB-)EVPN and (PBB-)VPLS PEs must coexist for the same VPN instance and single-homed segments.
  • Single-active redundancy must be supported for multihomed networks and devices on (PBB-)EVPN PEs.

All-active redundancy is not applicable to VPLS and PBB-VPLS, and support for it across both kinds of PE is outside the scope of the document. EVPN PEs that need to work with VPLS PEs MUST therefore use Single-Active mode.
sections.eli5: The rules are: move one house at a time, never ask the old houses to change anything, and let each family have just one front door in use at a time.

sections.title: Discovering Who Speaks EVPN
sections.content:
All the integration logic resides on the EVPN PEs. They must support BGP EVPN routes per RFC 7432 and VPLS auto-discovery (A-D) per RFC 6074. The VPLS PEs only need VPLS A-D. If a VPLS instance does not use VPLS A-D, EVPN PEs can still integrate it by manually configuring pseudowires, but the integration is then no longer seamless.

An EVPN PE MUST advertise both the BGP VPLS A-D route and the EVPN Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag (IMET) route for a VPN instance. VPLS PEs advertise only the VPLS A-D route. An operator may use one Route Target for both networks, in which case a VPLS PE ignores the EVPN IMET route as belonging to an unknown SAFI. Or the operator may use two Route Targets and RT Constrain (RFC 4684) to keep EVPN routes away from VPLS PEs.

When an EVPN PE receives both a VPLS A-D route and an EVPN IMET route from the same remote PE for the same VPN instance, it MUST prefer the EVPN route. After discovery, EVPN PEs know every PE and whether it is EVPN-capable or VPLS-only, while VPLS PEs see everyone as a VPLS-only PE.
sections.eli5: New routers wave two flags, an old one and a new one. Old routers only notice the old flag. When two new routers meet, they use the new flag and ignore the old one.

sections.title: Forwarding and Unicast Operation
sections.content:
On the EVPN PE, the rules are:

  • It MUST establish a pseudowire (PW) to each remote PE from which it has received only a VPLS A-D route. The PW runs between the VSI of the VPLS PE and the MAC-VRF of the EVPN PE.
  • It MUST set up the label stack for the MP2P VPN unicast FEC to any remote PE that advertised an EVPN IMET route.
  • If a VPLS A-D route arrives first and an EVPN IMET route from the same PE arrives later, the PW MUST be brought operationally down. If the IMET route comes first, the PW is set up but MUST be kept operationally down.

Customer MAC addresses (C-MACs) learned over VPLS PWs are learned in the data plane and MUST be injected into the bridge table of the MAC-VRF. They MUST NOT be advertised in the control plane to remote EVPN PEs, because every EVPN PE can talk directly to every VPLS PE and learns them itself. C-MACs learned on local attachment circuits MUST be injected into the MAC-VRF and advertised using BGP EVPN routes.

On a link failure in a single-active Ethernet segment, the EVPN PEs MUST both send a BGP mass withdraw to EVPN peers and follow the existing VPLS MAC Flush procedures with VPLS peers.
sections.eli5: A new router builds a private hallway to each old router and uses the fast new road to other new routers. If it ever finds out an old-looking neighbor is really a new router, it closes the hallway and uses the new road.

sections.title: MAC Mobility and Multicast
sections.content:
Host addresses can move between EVPN PEs or between EVPN and VPLS PEs. When a C-MAC moves from an EVPN PE to a VPLS PE, broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast (BUM) traffic from that address floods to every PE, and receivers update their tables. If only known unicast traffic is sent, traffic to the moved address can be black-holed until BUM traffic from it appears, for example after the MAC age-out timer expires. The RFC notes this is typical for VPLS PEs.

When a C-MAC moves from a VPLS PE to an EVPN PE, the address is learned and advertised in BGP, and the MAC mobility procedure runs among EVPN PEs. VPLS PEs may keep stale information and black-hole traffic until BUM traffic from the moved address arrives.

For multicast with ingress replication, the EVPN PE keeps one replication list per VPN instance. It is the union of sub-list A (MP2P service tunnels to remote EVPN PEs, built from IMET routes) and sub-list B (PWs to remote VPLS PEs). Split horizon MUST be enabled across all entries, both PWs and service tunnels. Multicast with P2MP tunnels is outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: If a kid changes seats, some friends may keep passing notes to the old seat until the kid says something out loud to everybody. Shouting out loud is how everyone learns the new seat.

sections.title: The PBB Variant
sections.content:
PBB-VPLS to PBB-EVPN integration follows the same shape. PBB-VPLS PEs need VPLS A-D, and PBB-EVPN PEs need BGP EVPN routes plus VPLS A-D, with all the logic on the PBB-EVPN PEs. Capability discovery is the same as in Section 3.1, and the PW and IMET precedence rules are the same too.

The differences are in what is learned. The PW runs between the B-components of the two PEs (per Section 4 of RFC 7041). Backbone MAC addresses (B-MACs) learned over those PWs MUST be injected into the MAC-VRF bridge table and MUST NOT be advertised to remote PBB-EVPN PEs. C-MACs are learned in the I-component and not advertised in the control plane, per RFC 7623.

There is no mobility for B-MACs here. If the same B-MAC appears behind both a PBB-VPLS PE and a PBB-EVPN PE, the local PE can deduce an anomaly and SHOULD notify the operator. On a single-active link failure, the PE sends a BGP B-MAC withdraw or a MAC advertisement with the MAC Mobility extended community, and follows VPLS MAC Flush with its PBB-VPLS peers.

For multicast, the PE keeps a replication list per I-SID: sub-list A (service tunnels to PBB-EVPN PEs) plus sub-list B (PWs to PBB-VPLS PEs). Optionally it may prune sub-list B using MMRP to get sub-list C, and then the list is A plus C. Split horizon MUST be enabled over all entries.
sections.eli5: The same trick works for the fancier version of the network. The new routers learn the old routers' addresses on their own and do not tell the other new routers, since they already know them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of RFC 4761, RFC 4762, RFC 7080, RFC 7432 and RFC 7623 apply directly, because this document reuses their control-plane and data-plane procedures.

The RFC says it introduces no new security considerations beyond those. MAC addresses in BGP follow RFC 7432, and MAC addresses learned over PWs follow RFC 4761, RFC 4762 and RFC 7080. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Nothing new here is risky on its own. The safety rules of the older documents still apply.
